title: John Flavell Named the Skill in 1979
author: I Speak Public
summary: This piece traces developmental psychologist John Flavell's 1970s research on metacognition -- thinking about one's own thinking -- and applies it directly to professional confidence and meeting performance. It distinguishes two components of metacognition, monitoring and control, and argues that professionals who skip the monitoring step become confidently wrong with increasing frequency as their intelligence grows. Central to the argument is the 'illusion of competence': rereading familiar material produces a false sense of mastery that dissolves the moment someone is asked to explain it without notes, because recognition and retrieval feel identical from the inside but are cognitively distinct operations. The author's proposed fix is a calibration ritual -- assign your confidence a numeric percentage before a meeting, test it by explaining the reasoning aloud without a script or running it past a skeptical colleague, and then state the adjusted, not original, number out loud in the room. The piece closes by noting that accurately marked uncertainty, paradoxically, is what makes a person's stated certainties trustworthy to colleagues over time.
points: Flavell's metacognition framework splits into two distinct skills -- monitoring (checking whether understanding is real) and control (acting on what monitoring reveals) -- and most professional failures trace to skipping one or both.
The 'illusion of competence' explains overconfidence walking into meetings: rereading notes produces false fluency that feels like mastery but collapses under a no-notes explanation test.

The proposed calibration technique is to state a numeric confidence percentage before a meeting, stress-test it against a real check (explaining aloud without notes or a skeptical colleague's pushback), then report the adjusted number rather than the original gut feeling.
Unchecked confidence compounds professionally -- a room learns within a few quarters which of a person's certainties have been tested, eroding trust in judgment even where it's warranted.
Self-testing beats rereading as the practical antidote to mistaking familiarity for understanding, since recognition and retrieval feel identical from the inside despite being cognitively distinct.
quotes: Flavell found the mechanism in children. As they grow they get better at remembering, and something else develops alongside it: they become aware that they are remembering, and they start steering the process on purpose.
The finding that should concern you is this: how well people monitor and steer their own thinking predicts learning and decision quality at least as strongly as raw intelligence does.
The illusion of competence. You read your analysis. You read it again. By the third pass it runs smoothly, nothing snags, everything is familiar.
Nothing was locked in. You were recognizing your own sentences on a page rather than pulling knowledge out of memory, and those two operations feel identical from the inside.
Intelligence without self-monitoring means you make confident mistakes faster, and a brilliant person who never questions their own reasoning becomes very good at being wrong with conviction.
Monitoring without control produces a person who watches their own errors happen and does nothing, which is its own kind of stuck.
A person who marks their own uncertainty accurately becomes someone whose certainties can be trusted, which is the opposite of what most senior experts assume about admitting doubt.
